messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas is a 63-year-old widowed man of Oceania descent who works in construction. His life took a devastating turn when he was physically abused by his romantic partner over several years, an experience that has profoundly affected him. The traumatic event involved specific instances where Thomas’s body parts were injured, and the mere sight of these areas triggers intense distress whenever they are visible or discussed. Thomas’s daily life is now a constant struggle to avoid reminders of this abuse. He finds himself jumping at ordinary sounds and waking in the middle of the night to check if he is safe. His fear is heightened when people related to the event are around, as conversations about it can swiftly bring back painful memories and emotions. As soon as Thomas enters any room or building, he scans for exits, a behavior that has become second nature but often leaves him feeling anxious and trapped. Thomas had come to believe that he cannot rely on himself in times of distress; his sense of weakness was deeply ingrained due to the prolonged abuse. These negative appraisals have led Thomas to engage in various maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. He makes sure to stay near an exit at all times, spending long hours scanning for escape routes during work and social gatherings. This constant vigilance has strained his relationships with coworkers and friends who find his behavior odd or overly cautious. In addition, Thomas turns to compulsive spending as a way to distract himself from the pain and emotional numbness he feels inside. He spends money impulsively on small purchases that offer fleeting comfort but do little to address the underlying issues. This pattern of impulsive buying has resulted in financial stress, adding another layer of anxiety to his life. Thomas’s fear of conflict also plays a significant role in his daily functioning. Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation is strictly avoided, as he believes he cannot handle such scenarios due to his perceived weakness. This avoidance behavior extends to work environments where disagreements are common, leading him to become isolated and detached from colleagues. The cycle of these maladaptive strategies has further reinforced Thomas’s negative appraisals. His compulsive spending and constant need for an exit have only deepened his belief that he cannot rely on himself or handle difficult situations. The triggers—like seeing certain body parts or hearing about the event—are now more potent because they remind him of the powerlessness and fear he felt during the abuse. Thomas’s life has become a web of avoidance behaviors and maladaptive coping mechanisms, each feeding into his negative beliefs about himself. What frightens Thomas most is the possibility that these patterns will continue indefinitely, leaving him isolated and unable to reconnect with others or find peace within himself. It was only after realizing the extent to which these behaviors had taken over his life that he finally sought help, hoping for a chance at healing and finding ways to regain control. Thomas’s current state reflects deep-seated fears of reliving the trauma and a desperate hope for relief from the constant vigilance and emotional numbness. His journey towards recovery will require addressing both the maladaptive strategies and the underlying negative appraisals that have become ingrained in his daily life.
